a: Evaluating security by safely trying to exploit weaknesses, with permission
tasks.fb: This is the definition from your matching task.

a: The organisation has given permission for the tests
The tester uses their own laptop
tasks.fb: Without permission it's a crime, however good the intentions.

a: Detects, blocks and removes malicious software
Sets who can see which files
Tests the system's security with permission
tasks.fb: Don't confuse it with a firewall: that controls traffic.

tasks.q: Why must anti-malware be updated regularly?
a: New malware appears constantly, so it needs new definitions
tasks.fb: Out-of-date protection is one of the ways people are a weak point.

a: Controls traffic entering and leaving a network using a set of rules
tasks.fb: It is the gatekeeper between a network and the outside world.

tasks.q: Which attack does a firewall help most against?
a: Unauthorised access attempts and suspicious traffic from outside
A member of staff losing a printout
Someone watching you type a PIN
A trojan already installed by a user
tasks.fb: Firewalls can't help with attacks that come from people inside.

tasks.q: What are user access levels for?
a: Limiting each user to the data and settings they need
tasks.fb: This is sometimes called the principle of least privilege.

tasks.q: A student's account is stolen by an attacker. Why do access levels help?
a: The attacker can only reach what a student can reach
The attacker is logged out after a minute
tasks.fb: Damage is limited to that account's rights.

tasks.q: Match each term to its definition.
pairs: Monitoring and analysing network traffic for information, evidence or intrusion detection
Evaluating security by safely trying to exploit vulnerabilities
A document setting out the rules a user must agree to before using a network
tasks.fb: These are the three definitions from your lesson task.

tasks.q: A company keeps getting infected by malware from downloads. Which helps most?
a: Anti-malware software, kept up to date
A penetration test once every five years
tasks.fb: Match the defence to the threat.

tasks.q: A company wants to find weaknesses before criminals do. What should it arrange?
a: A denial-of-service attack on a rival
tasks.fb: Testing with permission is the professional way to find holes.

tasks.q: Match each prevention method to its description.
pairs: Safely trying to exploit weaknesses, with permission, to find them first
Detects, blocks and removes malicious software
Controls traffic entering and leaving a network using rules
Limits each user to the data and settings their role needs
Monitors and analyses traffic to detect intrusions and gather evidence
Rules a user agrees to before being allowed on the network
tasks.fb: Learn these six, then lesson 10 adds passwords, encryption and physical security.

info.title: Bug bounties
info.text: Big companies pay 'bug bounties' to anyone who reports a security flaw responsibly. Some researchers earn a full-time living this way.

info.title: Red team, blue team
info.text: In large organisations, a red team attacks and a blue team defends, so both sides practise against a real opponent.

info.title: Zero-day
info.text: A 'zero-day' is a weakness nobody has patched yet. Anti-malware may miss it, which is why behaviour monitoring matters.

info.title: Two firewalls
info.text: Many networks have a hardware firewall at the boundary and software firewalls on each computer, so one mistake isn't fatal.

info.title: Least privilege
info.text: Giving everyone the minimum access they need is called the principle of least privilege. It's one of the oldest rules in security.

info.title: Logs matter
info.text: After an incident, logs are what let investigators work out what happened, which accounts were used and what was taken.
